meta.theme: the printed interview explained as a device that moves the custody of a statement from the paper to a named speaker, supported by the emptiness of the early specimens and by the form of the objection made against it, and conceded the occasional disclosure that nothing else would have produced while denying that a rare outcome can account for a universal form

meta.reviewer_notes: The rejected explanation is the one every reader arrives holding, so it stays available as an answer throughout. The passage's two supports are of different kinds, an absence of news and the shape of a contemporary objection, and the final paragraph concedes the rival's best case before pointing out that a rare event cannot explain a universal practice.

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option that an interview containing nothing new has failed at what the form is for, which is what the rejected explanation would predict and what the last paragraph explicitly denies with the words emptiness does not damage it. Q2's rival is the option calling the emptiness an objection the author later answers; the passage uses it in the opposite direction, as the first reason for saying the news explanation fits the form badly, and the only thing conceded at the close is the occasional real disclosure. Q3's rival is the option about journalism becoming less answerable, which takes a true consequence of the thesis and offers it as the thesis; the passage never evaluates journalism, and that option leaves the whole of the paragraph about emptiness with nothing to do. Q4's exception is the claim that early practitioners defended the form as more democratic, which is the kind of defence such a form usually attracts and which this passage never records; the other three are the second, third and fourth paragraphs in other words.

paragraphs.text: Before the middle of the nineteenth century a newspaper did not ask a public man what he thought. It reported what he had said in a chamber or from a platform, printed his letters, and otherwise wrote about him in its own voice. The interview, an exchange of questions and answers taken down and printed under the name of the man who answered, was an invention, and it was received as one. Editors on both sides of the Atlantic called it an impertinence, and eminent persons refused for years to submit to it. The explanation usually offered for its arrival is that it was a better way of getting news. That explanation fits the form badly.

It fits badly because the early specimens contain so little news. Read them now and they are conspicuously empty: a distinguished man is asked whether he is well, whether he finds the city altered, what he makes of the season's politics, and he answers like somebody who settled in advance what he would say. Almost nothing he discloses could not have been had from a letter, and a good deal of it had already been said from a platform. What the reader is given that he could not have had before is not a fact but an occasion: a named person answering a question he did not write, at a moment somebody else chose.

The second thing the form supplies is of more use to the newspaper than to the reader. An interview changes the custody of a statement. A paper that prints a claim in its own voice has taken responsibility for it and must stand behind it; a paper that prints the same claim within quotation marks, attributed to a named man who said it aloud before a witness, has published something whose truth it never undertook to guarantee. It has undertaken only that the words were spoken. That is why the device was useful long before it was respectable, and why the papers that seized on it first were those with the most to print and the least means of checking it.

The resistance to it is evidence for the same account. The complaint made at the time was not that interviews were inaccurate, which is what one would expect if the form were a way of collecting facts. It was that a man's words were his own until he chose to release them, and that the interview took them at a moment of his interlocutor's choosing. That is an objection about ownership and about timing rather than about truth, and it names with some precision the thing the device had altered.

Something should be granted to the older explanation before it is put aside. Interviews do occasionally produce what nothing else would: a sentence the subject would never have written, an admission drawn out by a question he had not foreseen, a contradiction visible only because two answers sit twenty lines apart. These are real, and they are rare, and the rarity is the point. A form that existed for them would be used where they were likely and dropped where they were not. This one is used everywhere, including the very many occasions when the subject says nothing he had not prepared, and it survives that emptiness because emptiness does not damage it. What the form was invented to deliver was never the news inside the answer. It was the answer itself, in a named voice, for which the paper is not answerable.

questions.target_mistake: judging an interview by the rejected standard, so that an interview containing nothing new counts as a failure of the form
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the inference will follow from the custody paragraph: what a paper gains is a claim it need not guarantee.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: The first interviewers were less practised at putting a question than the reporters who came after them were.
options.B: A paper unable to check a claim has reason to print it in quotation marks instead of in its own voice.
options.C: An interview in which the subject discloses nothing new has failed at the thing the form exists for.
options.D: The public men who refused to be interviewed were guarding themselves against being misquoted in print.

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph contains the whole mechanism in two sentences. A claim printed in the paper's own voice carries the paper's responsibility; the same claim inside quotation marks carries only the undertaking that the words were spoken. The paragraph then names the papers that took the form up first as those with the least means of checking anything.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option runs that mechanism forward one step. If attribution converts a guarantee of truth into a guarantee of utterance, then the less able a paper is to establish truth, the more valuable the conversion is to it. The passage supplies both halves, the change in what is undertaken and the kind of paper for which that change mattered most, and the inference joins them without adding a judgement about whether the practice is defensible.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question rewards joining two sentences the author left in the same paragraph without drawing the line between them. Look for a stated mechanism and a stated fact that the mechanism explains.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage says what an institution undertakes and what it does not, ask who benefits from the difference. Supported inferences in this kind of passage almost always lie in that gap rather than in a verdict on the practice.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing is said about the skill of any interviewer. The emptiness of the early specimens is explained by the subject, who answers like somebody who settled in advance what he would say, and by the fact that little in the form required news at all.
distractors.seductive_element: A reader who has accepted that the early interviews were poor looks for a cause, and inexperience is the first cause anybody reaches for in a history of a new practice.

distractors.why_wrong: The final paragraph says the opposite in as many words: the form is used on the very many occasions when the subject says nothing he had not prepared, and it survives that emptiness because emptiness does not damage it.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it is exactly what the rejected explanation predicts, and because every reader arrives holding that explanation and is never asked to abandon it in so many words.

distractors.why_wrong: The refusal is real and the reason attached to it is the one the fourth paragraph rules out. The complaint made at the time was not that interviews were inaccurate but that a man's words were his own until he chose to release them.
distractors.seductive_element: Misquotation is the standard modern grievance against the form, so a reader supplies it without noticing that the passage has already named a different one.

questions.target_mistake: treating the absence of news in the early interviews as an embarrassment for the author's account rather than as his first argument for it
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the emptiness is offered as proof, because a device invented to collect news would not have survived collecting none.
questions.stem: The relation between the emptiness of the early interviews and the author's account of the form is best described as one in which the emptiness is

options.A: the first evidence for that account, since a form for gathering news would not outlive gathering none
options.B: an objection to that account which the closing paragraph is written in order to answer
options.C: the reason public men could in the end be persuaded to sit for the earliest interviews despite their misgivings
options.D: proof that the interview was a poorer source of news than the printed letter it gradually displaced

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph opens with the word because and attaches itself to the sentence before it, which says the news explanation fits the form badly. Everything that follows, the health, the changed city, the season's politics, is offered as a reason for that verdict rather than as a problem the author has to deal with.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option gives the emptiness its actual job. A form said to exist for news ought to disappear when it produces none, and the passage's point is that this one did not, which is why the last paragraph can treat the same emptiness as harmless. The relation is evidence to conclusion, and the conclusion is that the news account is the wrong account.
explanation.question_type_note: A relationship question asks which of two things holds up the other. The connective at the join usually settles it, and here the paragraph begins by explaining a verdict already delivered.
explanation.reading_habit: When a paragraph opens by completing the sentence before it, read the two as one claim with its reason attached. Options that turn such a paragraph into a difficulty have reversed the direction of support.

distractors.why_wrong: The closing paragraph concedes something quite different, namely that interviews occasionally produce a disclosure nothing else would have produced. It does not defend the emptiness, it uses it, saying the form survives because emptiness does not damage it.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the final paragraph really does contain a concession, and a reader who registers the concession without checking its subject will attach it to the most awkward-looking fact in the passage.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage never explains why anyone agreed to be interviewed. It records that eminent persons refused for years, and the only motives it examines belong to the newspaper rather than to the subject.
distractors.seductive_element: An interview that demands nothing does sound easy to consent to, and the passage's stress on prepared answers invites the reader to complete a story about willing subjects.

distractors.why_wrong: No such ranking is made and nothing is said to have been displaced. The letter appears once, as a measure of how little the early interviews disclosed, and the passage's argument is about what the form was for rather than about which source yields more.
distractors.seductive_element: The sentence about the letter really does say the interview added nothing, which is one short step from saying it added less, and the option borrows the passage's own comparison to take that step.

questions.target_mistake: offering a consequence of the author's account, or the explanation he rejects, as the claim the passage argues for
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say in one sentence: the interview exists to give a paper a named voice whose truth it has not guaranteed, which is why empty interviews do it no harm.
questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: The interview was resisted by eminent men who held that a public figure's words remained his own until he chose to release them
options.B: Newspapers took up the interview because it was the quickest and surest way of discovering what powerful people actually thought
options.C: The interview was invented to supply an attributed voice the paper is not answerable for, which is why its emptiness of news never counted against it
options.D: Journalism became less answerable for what it printed once any claim could be attributed to a named speaker, and that is why the form spread as quickly as it did

explanation.expert_notice: The passage names its target in the first paragraph, calls the usual explanation a bad fit, and then supplies two supports and a concession. A main idea has to need all four movements: the emptiness, the custody, the shape of the objection, and the rarity that the concession turns into an argument.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option carries the claim and the test together. The claim is that the form delivers an answer in a named voice for which the paper is not answerable, which is the passage's closing sentence; the test is that emptiness does no damage, which is what the second and fifth paragraphs establish between them. Take away either half and one of the passage's own arguments has nothing to do.
explanation.question_type_note: In a thesis-and-support passage the main idea is the thesis at the altitude the supports were gathered for. An option one level below names a support; one level above names a consequence the author never argued.
explanation.reading_habit: Test each candidate by asking which paragraph it makes unnecessary. The right option leaves every paragraph with a job, including the one that concedes.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the fourth paragraph, which is one of two supports, and it is used there to show what the objection reveals about the device rather than to make a point about resistance. Offered as the thesis it leaves the paragraphs on emptiness and on custody with nothing to support.
distractors.seductive_element: It is accurate, it quotes the most human moment in the passage, and resistance to a new practice is the sort of thing a historical piece is usually about.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the explanation the first paragraph names as the usual one and immediately says fits the form badly. Everything after that sentence is written to take it apart, and the final paragraph grants it only the rare disclosure before setting it aside.
distractors.seductive_element: Every reader arrives holding this account, and the passage is careful to concede that interviews sometimes do produce what nothing else would.

distractors.why_wrong: A consequence of the account is being offered as the account. The passage explains what the paper undertakes and what it does not, and never delivers a verdict on the standing of journalism or explains the form's spread by its own decline.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it uses the passage's own closing word and states something that genuinely follows, which makes an inference feel like a summary.

questions.target_mistake: accepting a defence the form usually attracts as one this passage records, because it is the sort of thing such a history normally contains
questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the interview in its early years EXCEPT:

options.A: Its early specimens disclosed very little that could not have been obtained by some other means.
options.B: It moved responsibility for the truth of a statement away from the paper that had printed it.
options.C: The objection raised against it concerned the ownership and the timing of a man's words.
options.D: Those who defended it presented it as a more democratic way of reporting than the old one.

explanation.expert_notice: Three of the four claims have paragraphs of their own: the second on how little the early interviews disclosed, the third on what a paper undertakes when it attributes, the fourth on what the contemporary objection was about. Nothing anywhere reports a defence of the form by anybody.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The exception is the statement about a democratic defence. The passage records only hostility from contemporaries, from editors who called the practice an impertinence to eminent persons who refused for years to sit, and it explains the form's usefulness from the newspaper's side rather than from any argument its practitioners made. A defence that is never reported cannot be a fact according to the passage.
explanation.question_type_note: An EXCEPT question is three verifications and one exclusion, and the exclusion is very often the thing a reader expects such a history to contain rather than anything the text contains.
explanation.reading_habit: Before choosing, ask of each option which paragraph you would point at. An option you cannot anchor is the exception, however natural it sounds for the subject.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second paragraph in other words. Almost nothing the subject disclosed could not have been had from a letter, and a good deal had already been said from a platform, so the claim is verified and cannot be the exception.
distractors.seductive_element: The option generalises two specific comparisons into one abstract statement, so a reader hunting for a matching sentence does not find one.

distractors.why_wrong: The third paragraph states this as the central mechanism, contrasting a claim the paper must stand behind with one it has undertaken only to have heard spoken. The option is that contrast at a higher level of generality.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage words it as custody rather than as responsibility, so the option's vocabulary feels imported even though the idea is the paragraph's own.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph says exactly this, and says it twice: the words were a man's own until he released them, and the interview took them at a moment of his interlocutor's choosing, which the paragraph then names as ownership and timing.
distractors.seductive_element: It reads like a period detail rather than an argument, and readers discard as decoration whatever does not sound like a claim.

vocabulary.meaning_here: an intrusion that oversteps what a person may properly be asked

vocabulary.passage_use: An interview changes the custody of a statement
vocabulary.meaning_here: which party is holding and answering for the words

vocabulary.passage_use: at a moment of his interlocutor's choosing
vocabulary.meaning_here: the person conducting the exchange with him

vocabulary.passage_use: for which the paper is not answerable
vocabulary.meaning_here: obliged to justify it and to bear the blame if it is false

mentor.challenge: You already have an explanation for why the interview exists, and the passage names it in the first paragraph in order to reject it. Notice where the author lets that explanation back in, and how much he lets in.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The printed interview is best explained not as a better way of gathering news, since its early specimens disclosed almost nothing and the form survives on empty occasions, but as a device that transfers the custody of a statement from the newspaper, which would have to stand behind it, to a named speaker, whose words the paper undertakes only to have heard, which is also what the contemporary objection about ownership and timing identified.
mentor.main_idea: Newspapers invented the interview, and the usual reason given is that it was a better way of getting news. It was not: the early interviews contain almost nothing that could not have been had from a letter. What the form supplies is a change of custody. A claim in the paper's own voice is one the paper must defend; the same claim in quotation marks is one the paper has only undertaken to have heard. The objection made at the time, about ownership and timing rather than accuracy, points at the same thing, and the rare interview that really does extract something cannot explain a practice used everywhere.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Newspapers have not always asked people questions. For a long time a paper reported what a politician said in parliament or on a platform, printed his letters, and otherwise talked about him in the paper's own voice. The interview, where a named person answers questions and the answers are printed as his, had to be invented. When it appeared, editors called it rude and famous men refused to take part.

Why did it catch on? The usual answer is that it was a better way of getting news. The author thinks that answer does not fit.

Start with the early interviews themselves. They are almost empty. The great man is asked if he is well, whether the city has changed, what he thinks of this year's politics, and he says whatever he had already decided to say. You could have got it from a letter, and half of it he had said in public already. So what does the reader actually get that is new? Not a fact. An occasion: a particular named person, answering a question he did not choose, at a time somebody else picked.

Now the part that helps the newspaper. When a paper prints a claim in its own voice, the paper is responsible for it and has to be ready to defend it. When it prints the same claim in quotation marks, attributed to a named man who said it out loud with a witness there, the paper has promised something much smaller: not that the claim is true, only that the words were spoken. That is enormously convenient, and it explains why the papers that grabbed the form first were the ones printing the most and checking the least.

The complaints at the time point the same way. Nobody objected that interviews were inaccurate, which is what you would expect if the form were about facts. The objection was that a man's words belonged to him until he chose to let them out, and that the interview took them when the interviewer wanted them. That is a complaint about who owns the words and when, which is exactly what the device changed.

Finally the author is fair to the other side. Interviews do sometimes get things nothing else would: a sentence the subject would never have written, an admission he had not seen coming, a contradiction between two answers on the same page. Real, but rare. And that rarity is the giveaway. If the form existed for those moments, you would use it when they were likely and drop it when they were not. Instead it is used everywhere, including on the countless occasions when the subject says nothing he had not prepared, and it does not suffer for it. Which tells you what it was really for: an answer in a named voice that the paper does not have to stand behind.
mentor.why_difficult: The explanation the passage rejects is the one the reader brings in, and the passage never says it is false, only that it fits badly and accounts for something rare. That leaves it alive, and it is the source of two of the four wrong answers. The second difficulty is the direction of the second paragraph: the absence of news looks like an awkward fact an author would have to deal with, and it is in fact his first argument, so readers who mislabel it answer the relationship question backwards. The third is the last paragraph, which concedes generously and then withdraws the concession's force with one word, rarity.
mentor.author_intention: To take an explanation the reader already believes, show that it accounts for the wrong things, and put in its place an account of who is left holding a statement once it has been printed in somebody else's name.

paragraph_journey.note: Papers did not always interview people. The form was new, it was thought rude, and the usual explanation for it is that it was a better way of getting news.
The early interviews are almost empty of news. What the reader gets is a named person answering a question at a moment somebody else chose.
An attributed claim changes who is responsible. The paper promises only that the words were spoken, which is useful to a paper that cannot check them.
The contemporary objection was not about accuracy but about a man's words being his own until he released them, which is a complaint about exactly what the device changed.
Interviews do sometimes extract something real, but rarely, and a rare result cannot explain a form used everywhere, including where it yields nothing.

mentor.tone_progression: It begins as plain history, becomes dry and faintly amused while quoting the emptiness of the early exchanges, turns analytical and exact through the paragraph on responsibility, and ends fair-minded but unmoved, granting the rival explanation its best cases and then measuring how few they are.
key_transitions: 'That explanation fits the form badly.' (close of paragraph 1): the received account is refused before any evidence is offered, and the next two paragraphs supply the reasons.
'An interview changes the custody of a statement.' (paragraph 3): the mechanism arrives in one sentence and the rest of the passage is organised around it.
'These are real, and they are rare, and the rarity is the point.' (paragraph 5): the concession is made and then measured.
mentor.misunderstanding: Readers finish believing the passage says interviews are a poor way of getting news, and then treat the emptiness of the early specimens as a criticism of early journalism. It is not a criticism; it is evidence, and the author's point is that the form does not need news at all. The second wrong model reads the passage as an attack on the press for evading responsibility. The author describes what a paper does and does not undertake, notes who found that convenient, and never says the arrangement is dishonest.
mentor.traps_summary: The set offers the rejected explanation as the thesis, a consequence of the thesis in place of the thesis, the author's first piece of evidence turned into an objection he must answer, and the modern grievance about misquotation in place of the contemporary complaint about ownership. Sorting each option into rejected account, support, mechanism or concession answers all four.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage says an explanation fits badly rather than that it is false, expect the explanation to remain available as a wrong answer to the end, and expect it to be conceded something near the close. Keep a note of what the concession actually covers, because the difference between the rare case an author grants and the ordinary case he is explaining is where most of the questions on such a passage will be built.
mentor.real_world: The same change of custody runs through anything published in somebody else's name: a report that quotes an anonymous official, a platform that hosts what it does not write, a broadcaster that stages a debate rather than making a claim. In each case it is worth asking what exactly the publisher has undertaken, and what it has merely relayed.
mentor.takeaway: Putting a claim in quotation marks does not make it truer, but it does change who has to defend it.
mentor.reflection_question: When you pass on something you were told, how much of what you are promising is that it is true, and how much only that it was said?
